nameStory: The Great Black Hawk gets its name from its impressive size and predominantly dark plumage that appears almost coal-black in flight. The word 'great' distinguishes it from smaller black-colored hawks, while its scientific name 'urubitinga' comes from a Tupi indigenous word meaning 'black bird of prey.'
description: The Great Black Hawk is a large, powerful raptor with striking jet-black plumage across most of its body. These impressive birds typically measure around 22-24 inches long with broad wings that can span over 4 feet across. They have bright yellow legs and a distinctive white band across their tail that's especially visible in flight. While they're primarily tropical birds from Central and South America, a few individuals occasionally wander north into New England as rare visitors.

idTips.label: Overall coloration
idTips.description: Almost entirely coal-black plumage that looks sleek and uniform, lacking the mottled or streaked patterns of most other large hawks

idTips.label: Tail band
idTips.description: Single broad white band across the middle of the black tail, most obvious when the bird spreads its tail in flight or perching

idTips.label: Legs and feet
idTips.description: Bright yellow-orange legs that stand out dramatically against the dark body, appearing almost neon when seen up close

idTips.label: Wing shape
idTips.description: Broad, rounded wings that appear paddle-like in flight, giving the bird a heavy, powerful silhouette against the sky

idTips.label: Size impression
idTips.description: Noticeably large and bulky compared to common hawks like Red-tailed Hawks, with a thick, substantial body that looks almost eagle-like

habitat: In their rare New England appearances, Great Black Hawks are typically found near water sources like rivers, coastal areas, or large wetlands where they hunt for fish and aquatic prey. They prefer areas with tall trees for perching and are most likely spotted along major river valleys or coastal migration corridors. Look for them in mixed habitats that combine water access with substantial forest cover.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant season when individuals might appear during migration periods, usually detected by alert birders checking hawk migration routes.
seasonality.summer: Occasional sightings of wandering individuals, often near major river systems or coastal areas where they may linger for weeks before moving on.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for rare vagrant sightings as young birds disperse northward from their tropical range, most often spotted during hawk migration monitoring.
seasonality.winter: Very rarely, individuals may overwinter in areas with open water and adequate food sources, becoming local celebrities among birding communities.

funFact: A Great Black Hawk that wandered to Maine in 2018 became such a celebrity that thousands of birders traveled from across North America to see it, generating an estimated $1 million in tourism revenue for the local economy during its month-long stay!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with dark-morph Rough-legged Hawks or very dark Red-tailed Hawks, but the Great Black Hawk's uniform coal-black coloration and single white tail band are distinctive. Remember: if it looks like someone dipped a hawk in black paint and added a white belt, you've likely found something special.
contextualKnowledge: Great Black Hawks are considered 'vagrant' species in New England - meaning they're far outside their normal range and shouldn't really be here according to field guides. These sightings represent individual birds that have wandered far from their tropical homes, making each appearance a significant birding event that draws observers from hundreds of miles away.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus regularly reported in New England, Great Black Hawks are most similar to other large, dark Buteo hawks like Rough-legged or Red-tailed Hawks. However, they're much more uniformly black than any of these species, lacking the typical mottled patterns, and their bright yellow legs are more vibrant than those of common New England hawks.
